subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, ANNUAL STATEMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the banking and commerce committee discussed not only this bill but Bill No. S-ll respecting trust companies. The bills are similar in form. I think we all concluded there were two main changes involved in the amendments. One would permit these companies to borrow 12J times the amount of their paid up capital stock and reserve, compared
Loan Companies Act
with a limitation of 10 times that amount under the present legislation. The second point in the amending bill which I regard as of importance is that henceforth it will be open to these companies in making their annual reports to the Department of Insurance to use amortized value instead of market value with respect to their holdings of federal and provincial bonds.
To deal first with the latter point, the utilization of amortized value, toward the end of our committee discussion this morning I think the superintendent of insurance expressed himself as being rather a market value man. May I say that I share his view. As a depositor, shareholder or under any other circumstances I should like to think that under ordinary circumstances the legislation provided for a report based on market value. As a layman in this field I think I could understand such a report better than one based on amortized value. However, we had evidence that the insurance act permits insurance companies to use amortized value. We know that when the Bank of Canada and the commercial banks prepare their reports they use amortized value.
I was particularly impressed by the fact that in the case of the majority of our large trust companies, which are not incorporated under federal statute but obtain the right to do business under provincial legislation, no such restriction exists as has been provided in our legislation. As a result, it seems difficult to deny the proposed amendment although personally I should like to see market value used as the basis in these annual reports.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, ANNUAL STATEMENT, ETC.
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend appreciates that the market value will still be included in the annual report.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, ANNUAL STATEMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
I was just going to say that the superintendent of insurance indicated that, as he was a market value man, he and his department would be very concerned about market values in such reports. Not only the amortized value but also the market value will be reported annually. While the amortized value will be the effective value with relation to the amount of borrowing permitted in proportion to capital and reserve, the superintendent of insurance as an efficient government administrator will be receiving reports including market values and will be concerned about them from the point of view of the public interest with respect to the administration of these companies.
As far as the other item is concerned, we do not propose to oppose the bill because we feel that so many other institutions engaged in business analogous to that of a trust or loan company and operating under provincial or federal jurisdiction are already

Trust Companies Act
free in respect of the relationship of their borrowings to their capital and reserves. The superintendent of insurance said that he felt for the present, and I would judge for the immediate future, it would be very unwise to make the opportunity to borrow any greater by further increasing the ratio between borrowings and shareholders' interests in such corporations.
But he did indicate he approved of the present bill, and so far as I know those associated with me are prepared to support the proposed recommendations.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCORPORATION, ANNUAL STATEMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
On second reading of these bills we expressed some serious reservations about them. However, after looking very carefully over what happened in the other place in connection with these bills, and after the very careful explanations that were given by the superintendent of insurance in the committee this morning, in the main we intend to support this amendment that is now requested. I should like to point out that it is my opinion that as Canada has grown in population and as our economy has expanded, there has not been an equal growth in the financial structure of Canadian trust companies or Canadian loan companies. Their capitalization has not developed along with the growth of the country and therefore has inevitably led, over the process of time, to repeated requests on the part of these companies for permission to increase the multiplying factor.
I think that since we have in Canada only a limited number of these institutions, and they have developed to the stage where they occupy a very responsible place in the economic well-being of Canadians, those men who are responsible in these corporations may well pay a little bit of attention to the future. If we are not going to have new trust and loan companies functioning on the Canadian scene, then they ought to give serious consideration to a broadening of their base and the issuance of more shares so that there will be more risk capital involved on which to build the superstructure that circumstances and events inevitably will call for building. Had we financial houses such as they have south of the border, we could never support an amendment of this kind because it would be harmful to do so. There would be a risk involved. However, since we have in Canada evolved a system of a relatively limited number of chartered banks, trust companies, loan companies and the like and since it therefore behooves us to do whatever we can to help these organizations to perform their proper functions, we will support this bill.

Our quarrel certainly is not with the stability of these organizations. I believe this amendment will provide protection for the people of Canada in its overall effect. The only point I wish to make is that I do not believe the basic pattern has developed as rapidly as the needs of the Canadian nation should have made it develop. I hope some attention is going to be paid to that.

Is the minister going to make a statement? It is a very large bill. There are a number of amendments of which we did not have notification in the budget resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any statement that I can usefully make at this time. Several weeks ago in committee of ways and means the house had an opportunity of debating, and did debate at some length, the resolution which was the forerunner of the present bill. As the house is aware, in that connection the practice of the house calls for resolutions on the important matters affecting the balance of ways and means. The annual bill to amend the Income Tax Act, of course, always includes a great number of amendments that are not foreshadowed in the formal resolution that is introduced with the budget and is reviewed in committee of ways and means.
In the budget speech I indicated that the bill this year would be a lengthy one and would embrace a large number of amendments. The bill is a large one, Mr. Speaker, but while the amendments are many in number, they are all of an individual or particular nature, with the several exceptions that we debated fully in the committee of ways and means. I therefore think that anything I might have to say could be more usefully reserved for the committee stage of the bill if there are questions to be asked or points to be raised on the clauses of the bill when we are in committee of the whole.

Under the rules of the house, Mr. Speaker, this perhaps will afford me my last opportunity of again appealing to the minister to think in the general terms of the gift of $10,000 which is proposed as not benefiting husbands or wives in the provinces of Quebec. We have discussed this matter several times and I wish that I could have been convinced, either by the minister or by anyone else in the house, that the provision proposed would extend the same benefits to husbands and wives in the province of Quebec as it extends to husbands and wives throughout the rest of Canada. I had hoped that since we last discussed the matter the minister might have submitted it to the Department of Justice for a legal opinion, which I certainly would have been delighted to accept, that the measure benefits the people of the province of Quebec.
Income Tax Act
The minister may have been under a misapprehension with respect to the question of community as to property in the province of Quebec. I should like to point out to the minister than even when husbands and wives are not common as to property in the province of Quebec, they cannot benefit by this provision. I should like the minister again to look at article 1265 of the civil code of the province of Quebec. Husbands and wives, whether separate or whether common as to property, cannot confer benefits upon each other inter vivos. They cannot make any gifts to each other.
Under the legislation before the house it is intended that a husband or wife should have the right to make a gift of $10,000 to each other under the conditions which the law provides. That is possible-and I repeat -in every other province except the province of Quebec. I have mentioned this matter several times previously but since this is the last opportunity that I have of appealing to the minister I ask him to consider carefully the suggestion that he is, perhaps quite unintentionally, discriminating against husbands and wives in the province of Quebec. Since I come from that province I am deeply concerned about the matter. I therefore again urge the minister not to discriminate, even unintentionally, against husbands and wives in the province of Quebec who are just as deserving as are husbands and wives throughout the rest of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this is also a bill that was preceded by a resolution. It also was preceded by some announcements in the budget speech of the minister when he introduced the budget resolution. In consequence, we have had some opportunity to discuss his intentions and, may I say, also some of his omissions in the legislation that is now brought before us. However, much and all as we are trying to facilitate passage of some of this legislation that has had a fair amount of previous debate and discussion, I do not think he would expect us to overlook some of the omissions in the bill that is before us.
It is a very large bill. We were given information to that effect and to the effect only that it was going to be large in wordage. I think most of us realize that a great deal of it is simply a matter of administrative requirement and legal language. We are all a bit surprised at some of the things that are not in this bill. When the new administration was given the overwhelming mandate for which they asked the people in several of the election campaigns in the past, notably the last one, I think we expected more from the present minister. He has always taken an

Income Tax Act
interest in this particular statute. I cannot recall that when he was sitting in opposition he ever failed to make some remarks, usually lengthy ones, when this particular statute was up for amendment in a budget bill. Most notably, of course, we remember the last time that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) when he was sitting as an independent member expressed his personal views.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not as an independent member.

As a private member. I used the word "independent" because I realize that today my hon. friend must associate himself with approximately 20 colleagues and that they must speak with one concerted voice. I do not know whether that is what is limiting the minister in this particular bill which is not particularly noteworthy in its changes or whether he has just not been able to sell his propositions to his colleagues. With the vast number of private members who are behind him and who would give him such assurance today of ready support for any of the propositions that he would advance in legislation of this kind I would have thought that the bill would not be so nondescript as it is.
The tax foundation had this to say about the present amendments to the Income Tax Act in an article by their director contained in the last issue of their bulletin, which was most helpful and was provided to the people across the country who subscribe to this authoritative magazine:
The 1958 income tax bill is an oddly assorted collection of bits and pieces, most of them minor changes which are to the advantage of the taxpayer. Many of the larger matters on which briefs had requested revisions remain untouched. However some of the changes give substantial relief in limited situations, a good many of those in the latter class of course Implementing proposals put forward in the budget speech.
I do not want to unnecessarily refer to the items we discussed previously, which were referred to in the budget speech and were subsequently adopted at the resolution stage, but if my hon. friend the minister, when he sat on this side of the house, was ever consistent and vehement and often very comprehensive in his analysis of the reasons for his views, it was with respect to the necessity of increasing the personal exemptions under this act.
I find from examination of this bill nothing which is related to that aspect of the matter, and I believe perhaps the last time the minister spoke, as always with great clarity and, I think, conviction-and there is no doubt that he was not one who left back doors open for the possibility of changing his mind

-was on January 24, 1956. The public had great expectations from the minister when he assumed office, as a result of the views he had expressed, and at page 474 of Hansard the minister is reported, and in fact I recall listening to him at this time, as having said the following:
-the present exemptions from income tax, $1,000 for single persons and $2,000 for married persons, are entirely inadequate and should be increased.
He had a great deal to say beyond those words in an explanatory vein and he gave advice to this house with respect to this point but, for the sake of brevity, I will not repeat his words at this time. However, this is a notable omission from the first budget of this minister when he has had an opportunity to fulfil some of the very clear and obvious indications from his speeches in the past. I am sure that the public expected the fulfilment of some of these policies if the minister ever assumed the role he now has.
There are other notable omissions from the bill presently before us. We can find nothing here about faster write-offs of new plants. I would have thought-although this was advocated by such influential colleagues of the minister as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees)-that this would have been something which would have particularly appealed to the minister at a time when our economy was in the doldrums. I would have thought it would have had an exceptional appeal for him and for his advisers, particularly when such enactments were being provided in some important countries suffering from a similar economic decline as that suffered in Canada today. I have previously mentioned that the United Kingdom felt this would be a useful fillip to their declining capital investment and to their economy as a whole in 1958, but since making those remarks I have found that in a desire to give a stimulus and a shot in the arm to the small business community of the United States, the country to the south of us has approved tax cuts confined to small business. In particular such measure relates to the encouragement of business investment in the year 1958, when things have been slow, by the intensive acceleration of depreciation.
In the New York Times of July 22 last it was indicated that such legislation was being introduced in the house of representatives and although I do not have the clipping with me, in the Sunday issue of the New York Times of last week it was stated that this particular tax proposal had received the approval of the United States Congress. As I have indicated, this related to small business, but in brief fashion I would like to indicate that the proposal was that the allowance would apply only to the first

$10,000 invested. It was intended that it would apply particularly to investment in the current year and would provide for a 20 per cent depreciation of capital investment allowance in addition to the regular ones at a time when the economy was moving at a slow pace.
In the case of taxpayers who provided a joint return, the opportunity would go from $10,000 to $20,000 and this was something which I thought had worked out before when the economy was following a down turn and which would have commended itself to the Minister of Finance when bringing down his budget in 1958. There is, however, nothing along these lines in the bill before us.
I also found that the tax foundation had reviewed our situation with respect to this downturn in general business activity and had circularized a great number of businessmen in Canada asking them what in their opinion would be most likely, tax-wise, to encourage them to do the things in 1958 which would be prone to stimulate our economy. It was said in reply, of course, that in the first instance a general tax reduction would probably leave for them some funds which in turn could be introduced into the capital investment and development streams and would stimulate the economy but secondly, they suggested an increase in depreciation allowances.
As a further criticism of what is not in this bill, I would say we were rather surprised that we were not at this time amending, and it is not proposed that we should amend, the sections of the Income Tax Act which refer to our tax abatement in respect of the provinces. I can think of nothing which has been done, no other measure with proper regard to the economic situation which might have stimulated capital investment to such a degree as if the new administration had carried out its announced intention of calling the provinces together to give them a better deal-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must register my objection to my hon. friend going on in this way. This is not the budget debate but a debate on the principle of the bill to amend the Income Tax Act. speechtext: I was listening to the remarks being made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and I am inclined to agree with the Minister of Finance that he is straying away from this particular bill. Mr. Speaker, I am not referring to individual clauses. I recall very well that you were in the chair in committee when we were discussing the resolution that preceded the introduction of this bill. I know you have given careful consideration to the debates that have taken place before you came to the house and since your coming here including those that took place on second reading of bills of this kind amending the Income Tax Act. Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will have to ask the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River to speak to this bill more closely. "We must not wander into a discussion of other subjects covered by other acts.

Mr. Speaker, if you
examine the Income Tax Act I believe you will find the close relationship between tax abatement with respect to income that might be collected by the federal government and the relationship of the federal government with the provinces. However, I indicated that that was to be dealt with in a brief way and I have said all that I intend to say.
You will agree, Mr. Speaker, that the Income Tax Act has reference to opportunities under our tax laws for facilitating a larger degree of equity ownership in certain of our Canadian corporations by reason of tax encouragement vis-a-vis those companies that might be controlled in the United States. Contrary to much that we have heard from my hon. friends opposite in the past I find nothing in this bill to deal with this particular subject. I find there is nothing to encourage processing in Canada of some of our primary products. Having regard to the recommendations of the Gordon commission which suggested one line to be followed would be tax concessions I would have felt that particularly in a year when our economy was not strong we might have found something in this bill along those lines.
I wish to return to a discussion of the attitude of the present Minister of Finance. One of the items he always criticized and invariably deplored at this very stage in debate, second reading, in the past when an amendment came forward with respect to the Income Tax Act was that our provisions in this statute permitted the Department of National Revenue, the tax collecting organization, to withdraw at source from salaried taxpayers what he thought was an unnecessary amount of tax in consequence of which he always pointed to the fact that after the tax year was over it was necessary to make refunds to a rather impressive percentage of the total number of persons who had paid tax at source. I find nothing in this bill to fulfil the aspirations of my hon. friend the minister in this respect.
I have heard in the past complaints from a great number of hon. members who are still in the House of Commons and who in former days were representing particularly farming communities, and largely from Ontario, to the effect that some of the provisions of the Income Tax Act were unduly harsh with respect to taxpayers. I think of the hon. member for Huron (Mr. Cardiff) who was with us a moment ago, the hon. member for

Middlesex East (Mr. White) and the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton) who represent farming communities. Over a period of years in this house they said we had provisions in the income tax law that were unduly favouring the administration not giving the proper benefit of the doubt to the taxpayer. I see nothing in this amending bill which indicates either that they have approached the minister with respect to these matters once the Conservative party took over the administration of this country or, if they have, that the minister himself has shown a warm response to the representations they may have made.
In the relatively recent past I believe greater attention is being paid by members of the public generally to the possibility of giving a tax break to women who are working outside their homes for a normal business day but who could not do so unless they were hiring someone to assume some of their domestic responsibilities at home. This subject is increasing in importance. I realize it has complications but I am sure the minister will admit that more attention has been focussed on this question in recent months than in recent years. It does involve difficulties but I know that representations were recently made in a forceful way by the Canadian federation of business and professional women's clubs. I would hope before another budget is presented to the house the minister would give this matter most careful consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I have followed with the greatest interest the expose made by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl). This is not the first time the hon. member has raised in this house the question of the status of husbands and wives in the province of Quebec. Liberal hon. members representing constituencies in that province share the same views. If I remember correctly, and I think the Minister of Finance will recall that, on a previous occasion when we discussed this matter we suggested to him that he should get a legal opinion from the Min-iser of Justice as to whether a husband and wife in the province of Quebec would benefit under section 41. The Minister of Finance has failed to follow our advice. It seems to us, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance would like to discriminate against husbands and wives in the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Shame on you!

Otherwise he would
have sought legal advice; he would have arranged matters so that husbands and wives in the province of Quebec would obtain the

same privileges as husbands and wives in other provinces of this country.
There is no reason, Mr. Speaker, why we should let this matter stand as it is because, if we did we would not be doing our duty to the husbands and wives in the province of Quebec.
The Minister of Finance is learned in the law. He knows very well that according to article 1265 of the civil code of the province of Quebec husbands and wives of that province will not benefit under this section. I shall now read article 1265 of the civil code in French. It reads as follows:
Apres le mariage, il ne peut 6tre fait aux conventions matrimoniales contenues au contrat, au-cun changement (pas mSme par don mutuel d'usu-fruit, lequel est aboli).
Les epoux ne peuvent non plus s'avantager entre vifs si ce n'est conformement aux dispositions de la loi qui permettent au mari, sous certaines restrictions et conditions, d'assurer sa vie pour le ben6-fice de sa femme et de ses enfants.
For the benefit of the Minister of Finance, I am going to read the article in English:
After marriage, the marriage covenants contained in the contract cannot be altered, (even by the donation of usufruct, which is abolished), nor can the consorts in any other manner confer benefits inter vivos upon each other, except in conformity with the provisions of the law, under which a husband may, subject to certain conditions and restrictions, insure his life for his wife and children.
We have told the Minister of Finance repeatedly that husbands and wives in the province of Quebec were not covered by section 41. He failed to follow the advice and suggestions that we have given to him in good faith to go to the Minister of Justice and try to find a way to ensure that husbands and wives in the province of Quebec would receive the same privileges from section 41 as husbands and wives in the other provinces will receive. We do not like discrimination. We like to be treated the same as other people are treated and, therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl):
That this bill be not read a second time until further consideration is given to the possibility of making the tax-free gifts from husband to wife effective in the province of Quebec to the same extent as in the rest of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall be glad to say a word about this matter, Mr. Chairman. As hon. members will see, clause 8 of the bill extends over several pages. It is concerned with the rules to be applied in relation to lease-option and hire-purchase
Income Tax Act
agreements. Clause 8 provides for a complete revision of section 18 of the act which deals with lease-option and hire-purchase agreements. In some agreements the lessee is required to pay substantial amounts designated as rental payments and is given the option to purchase the property for a nominal sum at the end of the designated period. It is frequently obvious that the so-called rental payments are really instalments of the purchase price. Section 18 of the act provides that these agreements are to be regarded as purchase agreements. On some points the present legislation has been found to be obscure if not ambiguous. The proposed new section 8 is somewhat longer because it spells out in greater detail what is to be done in a variety of circumstances.
I can assure the house that it is the opinion of the government that these elaborations contained in clause 8 do not change the accepted interpretations of the present law. I believe that those taxpayers who are affected by the section will be pleased to have the rules specified more clearly.
The proposed revision includes two substantive changes. It contains special provision for cases where the lessor and the lessee are not dealing at arm's length, thus bringing the section in line with the other rules in the act covering other purchases and sales that are not at arm's length and blocking a possible loophole.
The second and more significant change is a provision that section 18 of the act will not apply at all in many cases. The specific provisions in this regard contained in the proposed new subsection 4 should remove from the application of this section all those cases where it is reasonably clear that the rent being paid is really rent and that no part of it is paid on account of the purchase price.

Mr. Chairman, in relation to these clauses we sometimes have a recommendation or at least a proposition that it would be applicable to either the current taxation year or an earlier year. I made some remarks on the resolution stage with respect to this matter of charitable donations deductions. A change is being made which will have the effect of widening the percentage amount of the deduction of taxable income applicable for a corporation. 1 continue to think that further consideration should be given to the position of an individual and, in particular, the averaging over a longer period of time to encourage individuals to make contributions of certain large capital investments in such things as universities. Universities frequently require large donations; they would like to go ahead with their capital programs and they appeal to an individual, who says, "Well, I must consider the income tax benefit related to this donation. If I tell you right now that I can give you in the coming year what you probably expect from me, I might find that all of it would not be subject to charitable donation deduction." I believe the averaging is for only two years, but certain contributions are expected from individuals for education generally, and I particularly have in mind that these capital requirements are often of a very large nature although they may not always be recurring donations. On the other hand, the individual also has the annual, continuing and repetitive types of donations.
In view of my remarks, therefore, it seems to me that some consideration should be given to perhaps extending the period over which individuals might average their donations.

speakerposition: stagedirection

The house in committee on Bill No. S-4, respecting the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company-Mr. Taylor-Mr. Rea in the chair.
On clause 1-Remuneration to directors.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: BURRARD INLET TUNNEL AND BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext: Hon. members may find the amendments made to this bill on page 437 of Votes and Proceedings of Thursday, August 14, 1958, as reported by the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Shall clause 1 as amended carry?

maintopic: BURRARD INLET TUNNEL AND BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as hon. members of the committee will appreciate, the ownership of this company with one slight exception rests in the hands of four municipal councils, that is the corporation of the district of North Vancouver, the corporation of the city of North Vancouver, the corporation of the district of West Vancouver and the city of Vancouver. In the standing committee it was requested that an attempt be made to ascertain the views of the four municipalities which in effect own the company with respect to the proposal in the bill. I wonder whether the sponsor of the bill could indicate what answers have been received individually from the four municipalities, what were the opinions expressed and whether there was any division of opinion in each respective municipal council with respect to the proposal in the bill?

maintopic: BURRARD INLET TUNNEL AND BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this bill reached the committee a resolution was passed in the following terms:
That this committee do not proceed with the bill at this time but that Mr. Taylor, sponsor of the bill be asked to communicate with the corporation of the district of North Vancouver, the corporation of the city of North Vancouver, the corporation of the district of West Vancouver and the city of Vancouver to ascertain the views of these municipal councils with respect to the bill.
Pursuant to that resolution I wrote to each of the bodies mentioned. My letter dated July 26, 1958, reads as follows:
Dear Sirs:
Re: Bill S-4-An act respecting the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company.
A resolution was passed by the railway committee of the House of Commons, relating to the above company. The resolution requested that I communicate with each of you to ascertain the views of each council with respect to this bill.
I went on to say:
When I was requested to assist with this matter, it was my understanding that the board of directors of the company had unanimously requested amendment to the charter of the company, enabling the shareholders in general meeting to make provision

Private Bills
ior payment to directors. The directors are all known to me and many of them have had long experience in municipal affairs.
Even if the bill is passed, it would not necessarily mean that directors' fees were to be paid. Whether or not they are to be paid is a matter for the shareholders to decide. It might well be that councils this year will be in favour of payment of such fees, while next year's councils may be opposed. In such event, directors' fees would not be paid in any year the shareholders were opposed to payment. Complete control over the situation lies with the local councils, who are the shareholders.
I understand that no director is a shareholder and the directors might not necessarily be holders of proxies at any annual meeting. The bill is so drafted that the directors cannot as directors vote themselves a fee.
Mr. Halford Wilson informs me that the Vancouver city council has considered this matter and that no one has opposed passage of the bill. It matters little to me whether the bill is passed or not, but I only hope that local politics will not be drawn into the federal arena. The bill has passed the Senate and has passed second reading here. I can only presume that the bill will not meet any further objection in the event that each council approves the bill in principle.
Pursuant to the request of the committee I trust that you will communicate with me as early as possible respecting your council's views.
In reply to my letter I received a communication from the district of West Vancouver dated August 7, 1958, to which was attached a certified copy of the actual resolution passed in council which reads as follows:
Resolved that: The council of the corporation of the district of West Vancouver which is a shareholder in the capital stock of the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company hereby approves of Bill S-4, respecting the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company and respecting the payment to the directors of remuneration and certain expenses as therein provided and hereby directs that a duly certified copy of their resolution passed on this 28th day of July, 1958, be given to the standing committee of the House of Commons on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
The resolution is certified by the acting municipal clerk of the district of West Vancouver and is dated July 28, 1958.
I also received a telegram from Reeve Richards of the West Vancouver council bearing date July 29, 1958, which reads as follows:
West Vancouver Council Monday evening unanimously passed resolution approving of Bill S-4 re Burrard Inlet and Bridge Company. Certified copy of resolution being air mailed to secretary of railway committee.
I have just read to the committee the text of the resolution herein referred to. I also received a telegram from the solicitor and counsel for the company. That telegram is dated August 5, 1958, and reads as follows:
Bridge company bill approved yesterday-
That would be August 4. I continue:
-by North Vancouver city council.

I received a further telegram from counsel for the company dated July 29, 1958, in which he stated:
Resolution was adopted July twenty-ninth by council of city of Vancouver approving Bill S-4 respecting payment remuneration and certain expenses to directors of Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company. Certified copy sent to secretary of standing committee-
I understand that each council has reported to the chairman of the standing committee and each has approved the bill with the exception of the council of the district of North Vancouver. That is the best answer I can give at the moment. The hon. member for Peterborough is not in the house at the moment. I attempted earlier to obtain copies of the actual resolutions passed by the other councils but I have been unsuccessful in this endeavour. I may state, however, that I have personally seen these copies.

maintopic: BURRARD INLET TUNNEL AND BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I
originally spoke on this bill 1 opposed it as sponsored by my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. I did so at that time because the purpose of the bill as set forth was to provide for the payment of remuneration to directors whereas, according to the shareholdings outlined by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, the actual objective of the bill was to establish payment for municipal councillors who were in effect doing jobs beyond the usual scope and call of their work. In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, they were merely acting in the function of councillors operating in a committee.
When the hon. member spoke on July 4 he made one or two statements which left a certain amount of doubt in my mind. For example, at page 1943 of Hansard he said:
No director is a shareholder, and thus a director is not entitled to vote unless he acts as proxy.
There was no indication at that particular time as to whether or not the respective shareholders in the company, which are the various communities surrounding Vancouver, gave a blanket proxy, or what type of proxy they gave to the members serving as directors. The directors, as pointed out by the hon. members, are members of the various municipal councils, one councillor coming from the city of Vancouver, one from West Vancouver, two from the city of North Vancouver and two from the district of North Vancouver. Since they were acting by proxy, I had a certain amount of doubt as to the authority of the particular directors and whether or not the respective councils had approved the matter or the bill, as suggested by the hon. member. To a certain extent my suspicions were confirmed at page 1943 of Hansard

in the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard where he said:
I feel that the directors have been most fair in considering the welfare of the shareholders. The directors could have drafted the bill in such a way as to have provided that they alone could have set the amount to be paid to them by way of remuneration but if hon. members will peruse the draft bill they will see that it is the shareholders and the shareholders only who have the power to determine the amount to be paid.
As the hon. member said in committee, a reference was made to the respective municipalities and municipal councils in order to ascertain that they were aware of this amendment to the bridge company bill which would in effect have given an additional stipend to municipal councils. This was particularly important to me because the municipal act of British Columbia forbids the payment of such extra amounts. When the matter was referred to the councils it was revealed that payments had been made for three previous years and in fact I believe the mayor of the city of North Vancouver questioned the legality of the payments. Therefore, upon receiving the reports from the various municipal councils, we were able to interrogate the solicitor acting in this particular matter, as well as the sponsor of the bill, and my change in attitude occurred at that time when I was assured that the municipal councils had been aware of the particular alterations and in fact three of the councils had approved the proposed change. Also, as the hon. member mentioned, the compulsory aspect of the bill itself, saying that the directors shall be paid a certain amount, was altered so that the word "may" which gave a certain discretion to the municipal council, was inserted.
Again, I must say in all fairness to the sponsor and the solicitor representing the directors of this particular company, that it was pointed out that the payments which had allegedly been illegally made were merely a matter of expenses as far as the commission and the board of directors were concerned and, in the opinion of the solicitor, were legally made.

He said: Mr. Speaker, perhaps the house would be interested in some information outlining the purposes of the bill. Stanmount Pipe Line Company is now a wholly owned subsidiary of Imperial Oil Company Limited. It was incorporated by special act of the parliament of Canada on June 28, 1955, being chapter 78 of the statutes of that year, with the power to construct interprovincial and/or international pipe lines for the transportation of oil in the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and outside Canada.
The object of the amendment is to extend the powers of the company in order to construct interprovincial pipe lines for the transmission of gas and also to extend the area in which the company may construct interprovincial pipe lines for the transportation of both oil and gas to anywhere in Canada. Although the company has no specific area in mind, it has carried on substantial explorations recently, as the company has stated to
[Mr. Broomed
me in letters of June 27 and July 18 of this year, and it desires to have this power or capacity in reserve. The company has stated it has recently drilled and abandoned a well in Prince Edward Island and is now drilling a second well there in search of crude oil. In New Brunswick surveys are now being conducted and the company plans to drill in that province in 1958. In the province of Quebec it has drilled and abandoned five wells in the search for crude oil. In the northwest part of British Columbia new oil discoveries are being explored and they give encouragement to a further search for oil there and also in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
The company feels that it would like to have the capacity to develop interprovincial pipe lines in areas in which it has not got the capacity to do so now. I should point out that the granting of this capacity at the present time does not give the company the power to go ahead and build pipe lines. It must appear before the board of transport commissioners and secure permission to build any particular pipe line it has in mind. This amendment really gives the company the capacity to do that.
The company feels that at the present time reserves of oil in Canada are well in excess of production but the limiting factor is markets which would indicate also the need of a pipe line. It might be of interest to know that in the last 11 years the Canadian oil industry has grown to a greater extent than any other oil industry in any other area in the world. Since world war II capital investment in the oil industry has totalled some $4,800 million.
It might also be interesting to note, in comparing our production with that of other countries, that although our industry is growing we still only produce three per cent of the crude oil in the world and we only have one per cent of known reserves. In 1957 the free world used some 15 million barrels of crude oil daily and petroleum has become the largest commodity of world trade.
I bring these facts to the attention of the house in order to show the importance of the oil industry in Canada compared with the same industry in other countries and to point out the necessity of this industry having regard to the development of our country. Stanmount Pipe Line Company is one of the companies that intends to extend the industry in Canada by investing further money in the industry which will aid the development of our country and assist in providing employment for our people, something we are all hoping to encourage. For these reasons I strongly urge that we give favourable consideration to the passing of this amendment.

If there are any questions for which I do not have the answers today I can inform hon. members that they will be answered by officials of the company who will be appearing before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines to which the bill will be referred.

Mr. Speaker, second reading of this bill is being moved in the dying days of this session and I would submit that there is little chance at this time for members to give adequate consideration to the measure. The sponsor has said that the Stanmount Pipe Line Company is now wholly owned by Imperial Oil Limited. This is another instance of what often happens to what is ostensibly an independent company at the time of incorporation. After it is incorporated it is bought out step by step by one of the big oil companies. I think hon. members should be very careful before they extend to Imperial Oil Limited a further monopoly of and vested interest in the oil resources of Canada. Imperial Oil is one of those companies that is not basically Canadian. It is part of an international cartel and I suggest that parliament should not give Imperial Oil this further control over the oil resources of Canada.
The sponsor of the bill has told us that there is no immediate need for it to be passed, that parliament is being asked to pass the measure on the basis of the speculation that oil may be discovered in Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick or Quebec. There is no certainty that if the bill is passed a pipe line will be built in the near future. I think we would be wise to wait until the next session of parliament to deal with this measure, at which time we could deal with it more adequately.
The Borden royal commission on energy, so the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) informed the house, is making an interim report to parliament on the oil and gas resources of Canada. I think it would be wise for the members of parliament to look at this interim report before passing on a measure such as this. The interim report has not yet been made public, and I do not know whether or not it is in the hands of the government. It would seem sensible, before we provide for the incorporation of a pipe line to carry either gas or oil anywhere within Canada or to export gas and oil, that we should have the advantage of seeing the interim report of the Borden commission because it is likely to provide a valuable guide to members of this house.
There is a war on in Canada between Imperial Oil Limited and the so-called independent companies. The independent oil 57071-3-240i

companies which are developing the oil resources of the prairie provinces are most anxious to extend their markets into either the United States or eastward to the Montreal area. The independent oil companies, the smaller oil companies, are the companies that are today developing the oil resources of this nation, but Imperial Oil Limited, which is part of an international cartel, is opposing the bringing of independent oil to the Montreal area. I am afraid that once the powers of this company are extended Imperial Oil may be able to use those powers or any charters which may be given, not really to develop the resources of this country but to further impede the development of the independent companies.
As I have said before, I see no reason why parliament should be asked to pass on this measure at this time, in the light of the pending report from the Borden commission; in view of the fact that this is a further extension of the oil cartel and because of the action of Imperial Oil in blocking oil development and the extension of the market for Canadian oil. I would think that in the best interests of the development of our national resources in an orderly way, this measure should be opposed at this time.

The sponsor of this bill now before us, Mr. Speaker, has made reference to Stanmount's oil exploratory activities in the province of Prince Edward Island and, as expected this year, in thp province of New Brunswick. I think that before this session of parliament concludes those of us who are concerned with the future of alternative sources to oil in the production of energy in Canada should make some statement in the house concerning the alternative methods of fuel use and of energy production in Canada. While on balance we will in most cases, I think, support this bill, I believe this is particularly necessary for those of us who come from areas whose economic livelihood is based at this time not preeminently on oil exploration but upon the future prospects of coal.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that one out of every seven dollars which is now being spent in the creation of new physical assets in this country comes from the expenditure of firms which are engaged in either the discovery, production, transportation or processing and marketing of energy in any of its forms. Some economists have estimated that this amount spent in the creation of new physical assets by these firms will rise to one dollar in every four dollars within the next generation. Those of us who are concerned more particularly with coal and generally with the other alternative means of energy production such as oil and natural

Private Bills
gas, feel that we should record why it is we can support a bill of this kind looking towards the extension of Stanmount's capacity to carry on the exploratory work with an even mind and without too much preoccupation by the government of this country with the extension of these alternative sources of energy. With all this expenditure, one dollar in every seven, Canada has never been and is not today self-sufficient in usable energy. Some economists measure a nation's national growth by the amount of usable energy which it possesses.
In 1950, eight years ago, we were then importing nearly two-thirds of all our fuel needs in this country. In 1955, the last year for which all the relevant statistics are available, I believe we spent $438 million on foreign exchange for the purchase of various fuels, including oil. If we were to account fully for our balance of payments on account of energy we should, I suggest, have to allow for the purchase of machinery and equipment used in energy import and also for payment to non-residents for such things as interest and dividends. We are, therefore, spending in this country today a large sum of money to import energy in some of its forms. We can measure our national growth, not only by the customary criteria of the gross national product, the growth of population, average wages, the increasing standard of living, but by the increasing use of energy, the use of coal, oil and natural gas, wood and water on Canada's farms, in her factories, in her homes, in her stores and in her mines. Those of us who are sent to this house to protect, defend and champion the cause of coal production do not want to be narrow-minded in our vision on this matter. We want to see the country prosper, and with it the people whom we represent and whose livelihoods depend in a larger part upon coal than they do at this time upon oil or natural gas.
A farmer in Canada can harvest today with power-driven equipment 30 times the acreage he could harvest by the use of hand tools at the time of confederation. A farmer in Canada today can harvest 30 acres for every acre he harvested in 1867. Paper mill operators turn out 10 times as much today as they did in the same period of time in 1900 as a result of the use of energy. To raise a ton of ore took two hours as recently as 1930; it now takes less than 50 minutes.
Mr. Speaker, some of us in the house are concerned with oil and natural gas but it would be understandable that in passing, at what we believe to be a late date in this session, or in giving support to a bill such as one asking for an extension of legislative capacity for Stanmount Oil, we are naturally concerned with coal. If I may be permitted

to enliven the declining hours of this afternoon's sitting, may I say that we are of a mind that there is no fuel like an old fuel.
Oh, oh.
It was the extensive possession of coal reserves which gave the first preeminence to the Ruhr valley. We do not need to go this far afield-

He said: This is a very simple bill respecting Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited which was incorporated in this house in 1953. When it was incorporated it was to carry gas and oil anywhere in Canada. The company now seeks permission to build a 30-inch pipeline from Edmonton down to just southwest of Chicago.
This pipe line will pass through Edmonton down through Camrose and across the Alberta border into Saskatchewan, will go along by Moose Jaw and Regina and will cross into North Dakota in the area of Northgate; it will cross from North Dakota into the state of Minnesota near the twin cities of St. Paul and Minneapolis, close to Rochester, and will then cross the Mississippi river just below the city of La Crosse and into the state of Wisconsin. It will then cross the state of Wisconsin and will go into the state of Illinois and will end at or near Joliet, which is southwest of Chicago.
It will be a 30-inch pipe line with storage facilities at both ends, and will have four pumping stations. The Canadian section will be built, owned and operated by MidContinent Pipelines Limited and the United States section will be built, owned and operated by a United States company which is a wholly owned subsidiary of Mid-Continent Pipelines and the majority of whose directors will have to be residents of Canada.
The complete control of this pipe line will therefore rest with Mid-Continent; the pipe line will be a carrier pipe line only, carrying oil from western Canada where we have a large exportable surplus of approximately twice the amount of oil we can use today and where, according to all forecasts, in the next ten years we will still have twice the amount of oil we can use. Detailed economic and geological studies of this area point out that last year the United States reserves for the first time dropped below their reserves in the previous year, 1956. Over the last ten years there has been a gradual decline in the ratio of United States reserves to increased consumption. Studies of the greater Chicago area show that the area uses approximately

Private Bills
an increase of 5.5 per cent per year as compared with the level across the United States of 4.5 per cent.
All the factors point to the fact that it is getting harder for the United States to find oil. Not only is it getting more expensive to pump but oil surveys show that the MidContinent Pipelines feel this is a great field for our exportable surplus of oil, particularly in Alberta and the other western provinces.
The initial output will be approximately 150,000 barrels per day and will gradually increase to 300,000 barrels per day. On the present schedule that will amount to $250 million in terms of United States dollars per year, and I am sure every member of this house will be very proud and glad to know that this would approximately equal one-quarter of our adverse trade balance.
In order to facilitate this project MidContinent Pipelines seeks certain amendments. Firstly, under clause 1 they have an authorized 5 million shares of no par value; they have issued 200,000 shares of paid up capital at 50 cents a share, amounting to $100,000. It is their purpose to further finance the project and further shares are to be issued for this purpose at not less than $1 per share.
To avoid preferred treatment for present shareholders, one out of every two issued shares is to be cancelled so that $100,000 of paid up capital of 100,000 shares is to have an average price of $1 per share. The unissued increase of 100,000 shares is so that the authorized capital will be restored to the usual 5 million shares.
We ask for three changes so that we can operate in order to sell this oil across the border:	Firstly, the capacity to operate
within and without Canada-21 of the 23 pipe line companies have already been granted this facility. Secondly, the addition of the words "extraprovincial and/or international" which are common to pipe line acts. Only two of the 23 pipe line companies are limited to interprovincial operation. Thirdly, we ask for the deletion of the proviso reading, "Provided that all pipe lines for transmission and transportation of oil and gas shall be located entirely within Canada". This has been looked after in chapter 37 of the 1957 and 1958 statutes on petition of Alaska-Yukon Pipelines and Mid-Continent seeks to have this proviso similarly deleted so that it may have complete control of this international oil line.
Before construction can start, however, permission must be obtained after an exhaustive and detailed public investigation by the board of transport commissioners. The licence to export the oil must also be obtained from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) .
[Mr. Rynard.j
I am accordingly pleased to move that this bill be now read a second time and referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for examination and report.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a comment on what has been said. The hon. member for Nickel Belt has quite misconceived the effect of the clause with which we are dealing. Mr. Chairman, it may be of some assistance if I inform the minister as to the value or lack of value of this amendment in paragraph (vi) in certain areas of northern Ontario, and especially in the riding of Nickel Belt. It will be very difficult for the taxpayer to realize why exemptions for certain types of transportation to hospitals should be limited to ambulance services or an ambulance.
In my riding there are no ambulance services and no hospitals except private clinics operated by certain companies. Furthermore, if you were to use an ambulance to travel from certain parts of my riding to the hospitals in the adjacent riding of Sudbury it would be necessary to travel for two days. The people who live in the lumbering communities in my riding and who are not receiving large salaries periodically, on the occasion of grave illness, must be rushed by plane or train to the nearest hospitals in Sudbury which would take roughly four to five hours. This is very costly compared with what people have to pay who live in well organized municipalities where there are hospital and ambulance services.
My people will be very disappointed to realize that this exemption is primarily meant to benefit the people in the metropolitan area of Sudbury rather than those people who live some distance away and to whom the cost of transportation to hospital means something. An ambulance account may be $5 or $10 at the very most but poor people living in remote areas must travel by train or plane to hospital and the heavy expense they incur is not covered by this clause.
For these reasons I feel that it will be a great surprise to the people of my riding when they realize that the amendment is meant to benefit only some of the taxpayers of the country.

Mr. Chairman, there was considerable discussion of this matter at the resolution stage and I thought the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo made a very important contribution to the debate at that time as has the hon. member for Nickel Belt now. I confess that when I looked at the resolution and certainly when I looked at the proposed amendment in the bill I felt, without meaning any offence to the Minister of Finance, that there was an undue Toronto complex in the design of this amendment. I see that the Prime Minister is in the house. I know that
Income Tax Act
he represents a remote and vast northern area like I do and as does the hon. member for Nickel Belt. The Prime Minister will know that in our sections of the country we have not got ambulances and that our people on occasion find themselves faced with an emergency where they have to engage the most available type of transportation. Transportation is not by ambulances such as the Minister of Finance would be familiar with in Toronto. It might very well be a taxi.
From my experience in the past I have found that taxi companies assume a great risk in transporting sick persons. There may be some chance of damage to the vehicle caused by the sickness but they always provide a car. I find that the air transport companies do the same thing. There is never any hesitation in making this type of ambulatory service available. It is always made available as soon as possible after the call is received.
I think the clause is unduly restrictive. I know that the availability of formal ambulances is increasing not by reason of the fact that there is any profit in buying an ambulance and making the service available to people in a certain community but largely by reason of the fact that funds have been made available by service clubs which realize that in small communities an ambulance service would not be commercially sound as a business venture. Service clubs have made ambulances available in such communities in the same way as they have sometimes made fire protection services available.
I am worried about the wording of this clause and I am a little worried about the experience of the Minister of Finance. I see he is discussing the matter with the Prime Minister and I think he will get some good counsel from him because he is well acquainted with some of the remote sections of northern Canada. I think we could readily provide an amendment to cover those who live in remote areas and, when they require immediate ambulatory service, are faced with an excessive charge. I know the worries of the officials of the department. They fear that people in urban areas will want to travel back and forth to a hospital by taxi and claim entitlement for a tax deduction. But in giving consideration to that element I think they have overlooked the very oppressive financial cost imposed upon people in remote areas who on occasion require this essential service. I think we could very readily amend the clause so that people who live in remote areas may claim exemption once, twice or more often in a year for the cost of what we know in cities as an ambulance but which in their case involves the

use of an airplane, boat or taxi because the ambulances we see on the streets of our cities are not available to them.

I wish to support the remarks of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and his suggestion to the minister that meaning of the word "ambulance" should be widened. At the present time it is far too restrictive. I am sure the hon. member has spoken from experience very similar to mine. My constituency is isolated and there is a lot of logging and mining. On occasion I have helped to bring out an injured man 9 or 10 miles on a pack horse. On another occasion I had to hire four men to carry an injured man a distance of 9 or 10 miles on a stretcher. On other occasions we have had to use launches over a considerable distance and in other cases logging trucks in order to transport people some 20 or 30 miles to hospital. On all these occasions there is an excessive cost. The purpose of the use of horses or individuals or vehicles is to get the man injured in the woods or mines to a hospital. There are a good number of locations in my constituency where there are no road facilities but only trails. These accidents occur in the course of timber cruising, prospecting and on some occasions trapping.
I cannot see why persons who live in urban areas should have a preference over those people who live in the backwoods. In the majority of cases they can hire a licensed ambulance. In the northern end of my constituency, injured lumbermen, injured miners, trappers or prospectors, are taken to hospital in what would be, from the point of view of this bill, quite unconventional ways. However, the expenditure in connection with that transportation is quite often treble the cost of taking a person to a hospital in a licensed ambulance over paved highways.
I do urge the minister to give some consideration to the representations made at the resolution stage, and again now, by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River with respect to giving those persons who live in the isolated and more or less undeveloped areas of Canada the same rights and opportunities under the law as those who live under different circumstances and who have an opportunity to use the vehicles mentioned in this bill.

When I made reference to the Prime Minister, I failed to mention that there is some form of free service to the sick in his province of Saskatchewan in so far as air ambulance service is concerned. However, I am sure he will be equally sympathetic to those in other provinces who are situated in a remote area and have not the advantage of a similar government

scheme. I feel this is very serious. I do not like to see in legislation anything that might in a transitory way appear to be a bit of window dressing, and ambulance service being included among the things that would be available for tax deduction in certain cases.
The hon. member for Kootenay West knows some of these vast areas as I do, and the situations are different with individual taxpayers. I have respect for the tax officials who have to examine the type of tax items that come before them. I think they have as generous a heart as any of us in this chamber. On the other hand, when a tax claim comes in they are inclined to define very rigidly what is an ambulance. This is what I fear. I think an ambulance is a vehicle that is clearly definable in large urban centres, but it certainly is not the kind of vehicle that, in many parts of my riding, would be used to bring sick persons down to the infrequent hospitals that exist in the area. I think the minister should reply to this.

I want to say a word on this subject. As this clause is written, there is no limit fixed in so far as transportation by ambulance is concerned. It may be five miles, 10 miles, 50 miles or 200 miles, and so long as the person is being transported to a hospital the cost of the ambulance is deductible for income tax purposes. Suppose a man has been hurt in the woods above Maniwaki. When he arrives at the hospital in Maniwaki it may be claimed he needs the attention of a neurologist. The nearest one is in Montreal, so they take the man to Montreal at a cost of $50 or $60. This amount will be deductible for income tax purposes, but the department will refuse to allow deduction of the cost of transportation from the more remote areas by train, by boat or by any other kind of vehicle. I think there is something which is not quite right about this clause. The department will allow the cost of transportation if the person is moved by ambulance, but if it is not an ambulance the department will not allow the amount even though it may be less than the cost of an ambulance.

Would it be possible for the minister to indicate whether or not in his opinion he believes the officials of the Department of National Revenue would be satisfied, provided this section is not abused by the taxpayer, that "ambulances" as defined in this section means such conveyance under emergency medical situations as have arisen, as conveyance by airplane, by boat or even by commercial vehicle?

The minister may appreciate it if I relate to him the fact that "ambulance" undoubtedly does not include a taxicab. However, because of the long distances in my riding, which I mentioned earlier, it has been known on occasion that childbirth has occurred in taxicabs. Possibly this is a case where the mode of transportation became at once the ambulance and the hospital.
It would be all right it if were made to read "by ambulance which is used for transportation".

Transportation is limited to an ambulance because it is relatively easy for officers of the department to verify. This matter will be studied in the light of experience, and there is no intention on the part of the department to give the new clause a hard or rigid interpretation. The matter will be under review, and experience will guide those responsible for shaping policy in this respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Clause 35 of the bill, Mr. Chairman, introduces new legislation with respect to amalgamations. It is desirable

that there should be clear and ample legislation governing the various features affecting income tax liability that arise when corporations amalgamate. The provisions here set forth in some detail are the clear statutory enactments that will govern these various questions that are bound to arise when corporations amalgamate.
The proposed new section 851 codifies the practice that has been followed in dealing with cases where there have been mergers of the type defined therein as amalgamations. This type of merger is possible under Ontario and Manitoba laws governing corporations and from time to time the taxation division has been required to deal with tax consequences of such amalgamations. It is desirable to state specifically the rules so that those who are contemplating an amalgamation may have more certainty in advance concerning their position.
The proposed section also provides four rules beneficial to the new corporations that are contrary to the practice previously followed. These are: first, the proposed subsection 3 permits a new corporation, under certain circumstances, to deduct drilling, exploration and development expenses incurred by its predecessors; second, any tax-paid undistributed income of a predecessor corporation at the time of amalgamation is carried forward as tax-paid undistributed income of the new corporation; third, where the predecessor corporations had undistributed income on hand at the end of 1949, but did not avail themselves of the opportunity to pay the 15 per cent tax thereon permitted by section 105, subsection 1, the new corporation will be given the right to pay the 15 per cent tax as though it had had a 1949 surplus of the same amount; fourth, where a predecessor corporation did not take advantage of section 105, subsection 2, which permits paying the 15 per cent tax on amounts matching its dividends, the new corporation will be allowed to regard those dividends as though it had paid them if it wishes to pay 15 per cent tax.

I think someone has properly said "on division". There was considerable discussion of this subject at the resolution stage, and on another aspect of it we had a division in the house today. We, in the opposition group, feel very strongly about this. I feel that the Minister of National Revenue perhaps explained very well the reason for this amendment to the Income Tax Act. On page 2136 of Hansard for July 10, 1958, the Minister of National Revenue said this:
From what I have seen in my limited practice-
I assume he was speaking as a lawyer.
-and I am sure others in English-speaking provinces have seen it too, a husband will deed a property to his wife as joint tenant. Perhaps they build a home when the husband retires and they create a joint tenancy. Then the husband dies and in the course of events it is suddenly found that there is a gift tax because the property is owned by the husband and the wife had not put any money into it. Time and time again complications have arisen because of the gift tax and gift tax assessments. It is to avoid cases such as that that this section is designed. It refers to the home of the husband and wife.
We did debate this question fairly thoroughly at the resolution stage, and in deference to the committee I do not want to repeat what I said at that time. However, I feel that there is much lacking in the section as it is designed. This is indeed a very general practice with respect to home ownership. This proposes that only when a land title transaction has taken place in the 1958 taxation year or subsequently will anyone get any benefit from this provision. Because of the very thorough review that was given to this particular proposition on July 10 and July 11 in our debate, while I felt that not very many members of the government party, although it is very large, actually spoke formally here in this chamber. I must say frankly that I had hopes that in caucus or by the utilization of other means they would have impressed upon the Minister of Finance the desire to amend this particular section. I felt ftiat the hon. member for Medicine Hat spoke in a clear way, as reported at page 2157 of Hansard, when he described the land titles holdings of this

Income Tax Act
nature with which most of us in Ontario and in western Canada are familiar. As to his part of the country he said:
We have . . . adopted the practice of joint tenancies in that part of the country and we have found that the principle of joint tenancy is becoming more and more popular.
He went on to say that with respect to joint tenancy in Alberta, should the husband die within a few years after the establishment of a joint tenancy, if the widow had not contributed or could not prove that she had contributed in a direct monetary way to the acquisition of this joint property, she would be subject to an income tax claim because of the gift tax provision. The Minister of National Revenue, who knows about these things, indicated that this matter was being raised steadily in his department. He indicated to the house that he felt that this provision would avoid all that difficulty. With the limitation that the clause applies only to joint tenancies in 1958 and onward, I suggest to the committee that we are not correcting the situation which was described by the Minister of National Revenue.
I raised the question on the resolution stage first of all as to whether our taxpayers across the land are likely to know about this situation before they die. Then I raised the question as to whether those who do know something about it are going to be obliged to go through all the legal rigmarole to transfer the existing joint titles back to the ownership of the person who could prove that he alone had contributed to the acquisition of the property and then the further rigmarole of bringing that property back into joint ownership in order to take advantage of the provision of this act.
I am disappointed that among the amendments that are presented to us tonight and as they appear in Votes and Proceedings of yesterday there is not one that relates to this particular section. I think that those members who have spoken recognize the problem. I am disappointed particularly that the private members on the government side who are familiar with this situation, such as the hon. member for Medicine Hat and I think the hon. member for Bow River, who also spoke about the growing tendency of this form of ownership of the home residence between husbands and wives, have not been able to persuade the minister to change this provision.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution contemplates the introduction of a bill which will be the final appropriation act for the fiscal year 1957-58. Today I tabled the report on supply for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1958. In that document we have set forth in great detail the position with respect to supply for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1958. If hon. members will have regard to that document, perhaps I can briefly use it as the basis for my remarks now.
Hon. members will see in the summary on the inside of the cover of the document that the total amount of all items which required to be voted-that is to say, excluding the items that we call the statutory items-amounted to $3,650,734,476. That is the amount left that required to be voted. It leaves out the statutory items in the estimates, the supplementary estimates and the further supplementary estimates (1) and (2), and also omits five items introduced by the former government in the spring of 1957 which were given continuing effect for the balance of the fiscal year. They are items 663, 664, 665, 666 and 667, and they are the ones which related to an increase in social security payments. By the form in which they were submitted in the supplementary estimates they were given effect, when adopted, for the full fiscal year.
Then there were two governor general's warrants to which reference was made earlier today which were passed in August, 1957,

one pertaining to assistance for the Hungarian refugees and the other to increased payments to veterans.
We also have to take into account the fact that both parliaments which sat in the fiscal year 1957-58 passed a number of interim supply measures. They are referred to in the same summary under the six appropriation acts which are enumerated.
What we have done in preparing this report on supply is therefore to take the estimates as tabled in the house, excluding statutory items, that is to say, all other estimates whether in the original estimates or the supplementary estimates or the further supplementary estimates No. 1 or the further supplementary estimates No. 2, and those are shown running through the entire document in the aggregate sum of $3,650,734,476.
In the next four columns we have shown how the supply was provided to meet each of these items. In the first of the four columns we show the amounts which were authorized in the various appropriation acts of which I have indicated there were six. The second column indicates the amount authorized by governor general's warrants with respect to each of these items. The third column lists eleven items which are of what is known as a transfer nature. These are items which represent moneys expended for which it is now necessary to provide, by transfer, for charging to another account. In the fourth column we have the total. There is a final column at the right-hand side of the page which accounts for the difference. In other words, it indicates the reductions made by the governor general in council except where indicated.
That brings me back, Mr. Chairman, to a comment upon the figures. Hon. members will see in the summary a figure of $114,065,172, which is the total of two reductions. They are composed in the first place of items 180, 184 and 399, and in the second place, of reductions effected by the governor general in council prior to the issuance of special warrants on February 7 by which supply was provided for the balance of the fiscal year to March 31, after the dissolution which occurred on February 1.
